paragraphs: A detector cascade organizes prediction into a sequence of stages, making its design a question of both recognition quality and computational cost. Choosing the stages separately can miss how these objectives interact across the whole detector. This paper develops a mathematical model that accounts for classification performance and complexity together, while allowing the necessary calculations to be performed recursively.

The proposed boosting algorithm, FCBoost, uses this model to automate cascade construction. Its objective combines classification risk and complexity through a Lagrangian cost, giving both considerations a role in the search. The algorithm searches cascade configurations to determine the number of stages and the predictors assigned to them. It also accommodates cost-sensitive learning and bootstrapping of negative examples.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across several computer vision problems. The contribution is therefore both a tractable way to describe cascades and a procedure for designing them automatically. The findings support treating computational effort as part of the learning objective when constructing a detector.
neurips-2010-boosting-classifier-cascade.tldr: FCBoost automatically designs detector cascades by jointly optimizing classification risk and computational complexity.

paragraphs: Multiple-instance learning involves classifying collections of instances, called bags, while reasoning about the instances within them. Its constraints have traditionally led to difficult nonconvex optimization problems. This paper changes the quantity being learned: it expresses the multiple-instance constraint as a convex restriction on a likelihood ratio, making a different optimization route available.

The authors show that a likelihood-ratio function and likelihoods on training instances can be estimated jointly through convex learning. They also prove a quantitative connection between the loss used for ratio estimation and classification error measured with zero-one loss. This establishes a theoretical reason to use the ratio-estimation objective as a surrogate for classification, alongside its ability to separate positive and negative instances.

The joint estimation nevertheless tends to underestimate how likely an example is to be positive. The proposed classification procedure uses the estimated ratios as features and learns a linear combination for predicting bag labels. Synthetic and real-data experiments report superior performance for the approach, supporting the usefulness of this convex reformulation and subsequent classification step.
neurips-2010-convex-multiple-instance-le.tldr: The paper reformulates multiple-instance learning through convex likelihood-ratio estimation and uses the estimates as features for bag classification.

paragraphs: Planning with a Markov decision process becomes harder when its parameters are uncertain. A decision maker may have some information about their distribution without knowing that distribution precisely. This paper represents such information through nested sets of parameter values, each associated with a probabilistic guarantee at a different confidence level.

Together, these guarantees specify which probability distributions over the unknown parameters are admissible. The proposed decision rule chooses a policy that maximizes expected total reward under the most adverse admissible distribution. Consequently, the policy accounts for uncertainty while still making use of the available prior information. The adversary is constrained by those probabilistic guarantees rather than being allowed to choose an arbitrary distribution.

The main computational result reduces this distributionally robust planning problem to a standard robust Markov decision process with a single uncertainty set. Under mild technical conditions, the optimal policy can therefore be computed in polynomial time. This connects a richer description of uncertainty to an established form of robust planning without abandoning computational tractability.
neurips-2010-distributionally-robust-mar.tldr: The paper makes planning under imprecise parameter distributions tractable by reducing distributionally robust MDPs to standard robust MDPs.

paragraphs: Q-learning estimates how valuable different actions are and uses the largest estimated value when learning. In stochastic environments, those estimates fluctuate. Taking their maximum can favor an estimate that happens to be too high, creating a positive bias. The paper identifies large overestimates from this mechanism as the cause of poor Q-learning performance in some environments.

The authors introduce a double-estimator method for approximating the largest expected value among a collection of random variables. This changes how the maximum is estimated and can sometimes produce underestimation instead of overestimation. The result is a different pattern of estimation error; the abstract does not claim that the new estimator eliminates every form of bias.

Applying this method to action-value learning produces Double Q-learning, an off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm. The paper proves convergence to the optimal policy and demonstrates good performance in some settings where ordinary Q-learning struggles because of overestimation. Its central contribution is to connect a specific statistical bias in value estimation to a concrete change in the learning algorithm.
neurips-2010-double-q-learning-e5beb24a5.tldr: Double Q-learning changes how maximum action values are estimated to address overestimation that harms Q-learning in some stochastic environments.

paragraphs: Animals can distribute their choices probabilistically according to previous actions and rewards. Matching behavior describes an observed relationship between choice allocation and rewards. Earlier theoretical work showed that matching could be a steady state when synaptic changes follow the covariance between reward and neural activity. This paper examines a feature that analysis omitted: changes in the entire distribution of synaptic weights.

The authors show that matching need not remain a steady state when synapses are strong enough for fluctuations from individual sensory neurons to affect the total input to output neurons. As synaptic weights diffuse, the variance of the input potential increases. Accounting for this changing variability alters the behavior predicted by the covariance-based learning rule.

The resulting effect produces undermatching, a phenomenon observed in many behavioral experiments. This connects a property of synaptic dynamics to a recognizable pattern in action selection. The authors suggest that diffusion of synaptic weights could provide a robust neural mechanism for stochastic choice, with the steady-state conclusion depending on the stated strength and fluctuation conditions.
neurips-2010-effects-of-synaptic-weight-.tldr: Synaptic weight diffusion can disrupt matching behavior under sufficiently strong synapses and produce undermatching in decision-making networks.

paragraphs: Feature selection aims to retain meaningful measurements while removing noisy or unhelpful ones. This is especially relevant to biological data, where the selected measurements may serve as candidate biomarkers. The paper proposes a regression-based feature-selection objective that addresses two requirements together: resistance to unusual data points and consistent selection of features across the data.

The method uses the same mathematical norm, the ℓ2,1 norm, in two different parts of the objective. In the loss function, it provides robustness to outliers. In the regularization term, it encourages joint sparsity, so that feature selection is shared across data points. These two uses connect the treatment of unreliable observations with the search for a compact set of useful features.

The authors introduce an efficient optimization algorithm and prove that it converges. They apply the method to genomic and proteomic biomarker discovery, evaluating it on six datasets. Those empirical studies support the method's effectiveness, while the convergence result supplies a separate theoretical guarantee about the proposed algorithm.
neurips-2010-efficient-and-robust-featur.tldr: Using ℓ2,1 norms for both loss and regularization combines outlier robustness with joint feature selection in an efficient, convergent algorithm.

paragraphs: Probabilistic grammars describe how structured observations can be generated, making them useful for data with sequential or compositional organization. Learning such a model involves choosing parameters that determine the probabilities it assigns. This paper studies that learning problem for a fixed grammar, placing parameter estimation within a framework for empirical risk minimization.

The learning objective uses log-loss, which evaluates the probabilities the grammar assigns to observed data. The framework uses approximations of probabilistic grammars and resembles structural risk minimization, linking the learning procedure to questions of model complexity and statistical reliability. Its focus is the estimation of parameters within the specified grammar rather than the selection of a new grammatical structure.

The authors derive sample-complexity bounds for both supervised and unsupervised learning in this framework. Such bounds address how the amount of training data relates to the statistical demands of learning. Covering both settings gives the analysis relevance to different forms of available supervision and provides a theoretical basis for studying grammar estimation through empirical risk minimization.
neurips-2010-empirical-risk-minimization.tldr: The paper gives a log-loss framework for learning fixed probabilistic grammars and derives sample-complexity bounds with and without supervision.

paragraphs: A pseudo-Boolean function takes binary inputs, while a convex relaxation allows a broader set of values to make optimization more manageable. Roof duality provides a familiar relaxation for quadratic functions of this kind. This paper asks what mathematical property should guide extensions of roof duality to functions beyond the quadratic case.

The proposed requirement is total half-integrality. The relaxation is polyhedral, and its extreme points use only zero, one-half, and one. Crucially, that structure must survive constraints that equate variables, make them complements, or fix them to one of those three values. This preservation requirement makes the property stronger than simply observing half-integral extreme points in the original relaxation.

The authors completely characterize these relaxations through a one-to-one correspondence with bisubmodular functions. They also give a new characterization of bisubmodularity and establish relationships with relaxations based on roof duality. These results provide a structural foundation for generalizing the method: they identify exactly which functions correspond to the proposed class of relaxations.
neurips-2010-generalized-roof-duality-an.tldr: The paper characterizes totally half-integral convex relaxations through an exact correspondence with bisubmodular functions.

paragraphs: Commute distance measures the expected time for a random walk to travel between two graph vertices and return. Because the walk follows the graph's connections, this quantity appears naturally suited to describing relationships between vertices. The paper investigates whether that interpretation remains useful as the graph becomes larger.

The authors prove that, in their large-sample analysis, commute distance approaches an expression that no longer captures graph structure. This is a problem for using it as a meaningful distance: a quantity derived from movement through the graph can lose the structural information that motivated its use. The finding concerns the limiting behavior of the measure, rather than merely a computational difficulty in calculating it.

On this basis, the paper strongly discourages using raw commute distance for machine learning on large graphs and in high dimensions. It introduces amplified commute distance to correct the unwanted large-sample effects. The contribution combines a warning grounded in theoretical analysis with an alternative designed to address the identified failure.
neurips-2010-getting-lost-in-space-large.tldr: The paper shows that raw commute distance loses structural meaning in its large-sample limit and proposes an amplified correction.

paragraphs: Finding the lowest-rank matrix that satisfies affine constraints is an important optimization problem in machine learning and statistics. The paper proposes Singular Value Projection, or SVP, as a simple, fast algorithm for this task. It proves recovery of the minimum-rank solution when the constraints satisfy a restricted isometry property, a condition governing how the measurements preserve relevant matrix information.

Under that condition, SVP has a geometric convergence guarantee even with noise and requires weaker restricted-isometry constants than existing methods. A Newton-step extension substantially improves convergence in experiments. The authors also report empirical speed advantages of an order of magnitude over compared methods, alongside greater robustness to noise and sampling choices.

Matrix completion requires a separate interpretation because its measurement constraints do not directly satisfy the restricted isometry property used by the main theorem. The authors establish a narrower property as partial progress toward exact recovery. Empirically, SVP recovers incoherent low-rank matrices from nearly optimal numbers of uniformly sampled entries, while SVP-Newton also performs strongly with noise and power-law sampling.
neurips-2010-guaranteed-rank-minimizatio.tldr: SVP provides conditional recovery guarantees for rank minimization and strong empirical results for matrix completion, where its main guarantee does not directly apply.

paragraphs: Recovering a three-dimensional pose from a single image is ambiguous because the image does not uniquely specify the underlying configuration. Physical constraints can narrow the set of plausible poses. This paper studies how to make the output of a learned predictor respect such constraints, using Gaussian process regression as its predictive model.

The first result concerns linear constraints: if the training examples satisfy them, the Gaussian process mean prediction implicitly satisfies them as well. This connects a property of the training outputs directly to the structure of the prediction. The result specifically concerns the predicted mean, so its scope is more precise than a claim about every possible output of the probabilistic model.

The authors then show how a change of variables can force a Gaussian process to satisfy quadratic constraints. Together, these results provide ways to incorporate physical feasibility into discriminative pose prediction. Experiments on rigid and non-rigid pose estimation report better performance than state-of-the-art approaches, supporting the practical usefulness of the constrained formulation.
neurips-2010-implicitly-constrained-gaus.tldr: The paper shows how Gaussian process pose predictions can inherit linear constraints and satisfy quadratic constraints through a change of variables.

paragraphs: Neural populations exhibit activity both spontaneously and in response to input. This paper asks how the spatial patterns of these two kinds of activity are related, and how network connectivity shapes fluctuations in an input-driven response. It compares how internally generated and evoked activity are distributed across the units of a network.

The authors develop an approach complementary to principal component analysis. Their analysis uses angles between subspaces to compare the shapes of activity trajectories in different network states and the orientation of the low-dimensional spaces occupied by driven responses. This provides a way to examine relationships between population activity patterns beyond treating high-variance directions for each input condition separately.

The methods reveal how spontaneous activity affects evoked responses and can infer input selectivity arising from network dynamics. The required spontaneous-activity measurements can be experimentally accessible through voltage-sensitive or calcium-sensitive imaging. The authors conclude that detailed maps of incoming inputs and cortical connectivity are not required to design spatially extended stimuli that evoke strong responses.
neurips-2010-inferring-stimulus-selectiv.tldr: Analyzing the geometry of population activity can reveal network-driven stimulus selectivity from measurements of spontaneous neural dynamics.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent needs estimates of future value to guide its decisions, but an estimate alone does not indicate how much confidence to place in it. Confidence information can help guide exploration and adjust parameters automatically. This paper studies how to obtain such information for value estimates in continuous-state Markov decision processes.

The statistical difficulty is that data from ongoing interaction rarely fit traditional assumptions. Value estimates are dependent, may have non-normal distributions, and can be based on very few observations early in learning. Moreover, the agent's policy changes as it learns. These features make conventional confidence-interval reasoning difficult precisely when uncertainty information can be especially useful.

The authors show how bootstrapping can compute confidence intervals online while the policy changes, and prove validity under a set of assumptions. They demonstrate applications to exploration, parameter estimation, and tracking. The contribution is a way to accompany evolving value estimates with statistically supported uncertainty estimates, connecting confidence assessment to practical decisions during learning.
neurips-2010-interval-estimation-for-rei.tldr: The paper develops bootstrap confidence intervals for online reinforcement learning with changing policies and proves their validity under assumptions.

paragraphs: Maximum a posteriori estimation seeks the most probable joint assignment in a graphical model. This can be a difficult inference problem, and linear-programming relaxations provide one established route. The paper develops an alternative by transforming the MAP problem into inference in a finite mixture of simple Bayesian networks.

From this mixture formulation, the authors derive an Expectation Maximization algorithm. Its updates monotonically improve a lower bound associated with the MAP objective until convergence. The update equations are simple and can be implemented as messages passed through a graph, in a manner similar to max-product computation. This gives the reformulation a concrete computational procedure as well as a convergence property.

Experiments on a real-world protein design dataset compare the method with MPLP, an approach based on linear-programming relaxation. EM converges substantially faster, often by an order of magnitude, and reaches solution quality within 95 percent of optimal for most instances. These are empirical solution-quality results; the monotonic bound improvement itself does not establish exact optimality.
neurips-2010-map-estimation-for-graphica.tldr: Recasting MAP inference as mixture-model inference yields simple EM updates with monotonic bound improvement and fast empirical convergence.

paragraphs: Separate organizations may want to combine what their data reveal without exposing information about individual records. The challenge becomes more demanding when the participating organizations do not trust one another or the party coordinating the process. This paper develops a protocol for constructing a differentially private aggregate classifier from classifiers that the participants train locally.

The participants interact with an untrusted curator to construct additive shares of a perturbed aggregate classifier. The protocol therefore places both distributed participation and privacy-preserving perturbation within the construction process. Its target is a useful combined predictor with a formal privacy guarantee, built from contributions held by separate, mutually untrusting parties.

The theoretical analysis proves differential privacy for the perturbed aggregate classifier and bounds the excess risk caused by perturbation. The risk bound addresses the predictive cost of introducing privacy protection, alongside the privacy proof itself. An experiment on a real dataset verifies the bound, connecting the protocol's theoretical treatment of utility loss to an empirical evaluation.
neurips-2010-multiparty-differential-pri.tldr: The paper combines locally trained classifiers through an untrusted curator while proving differential privacy and bounding perturbation-induced excess risk.

paragraphs: Pixels and local image patches can support effective visual recognition, but they contain little explicit semantic meaning. For tasks such as scene classification, a representation organized around objects may provide more useful information. This paper introduces Object Bank, a way to describe an image through the responses of a large collection of pretrained generic object detectors.

The representation takes the form of a scale-invariant response map. The detectors are pretrained without knowledge of the testing dataset or target visual task, so the resulting representation draws on generic object information. This changes the features supplied to a classifier: the learning system receives object-detector responses as its description of an image.

The authors report superior performance on high-level recognition tasks using ordinary classifiers, including logistic regression and linear support vector machines. Sparsity algorithms improve efficiency and scalability for large scene datasets while revealing meaningful semantic feature patterns. The findings show how investing in the image representation can make relatively simple classifiers effective on tasks requiring higher-level visual information.
neurips-2010-object-bank-a-high-level-im.tldr: Object Bank represents images with generic object-detector responses, enabling strong high-level recognition with simple classifiers.

paragraphs: In a repeated zero-sum game, a player's best strategy depends on what the opponent is allowed to do over time. This paper considers adversaries whose sequences of actions must obey a budget constraint. The player knows that constraint and seeks an appropriate mixed strategy, meaning a strategy that randomizes its choices.

The central question is how to exploit the budget while still protecting against the strongest permitted opponent. For a general class of normal-form games, the authors show that the minimax strategy can be computed efficiently. Their algorithm relies on a random-playout technique, providing a computational template for incorporating constraints on the adversary's overall sequence of actions.

The paper applies this template to three different settings: a cost-sensitive version of Hedge, a particular problem in metrical task systems, and combinatorial prediction-market design. These applications demonstrate the range of the formulation. The result gives known adversarial constraints a direct algorithmic role in selecting a strategy, with efficiency established for the stated class of games.
neurips-2010-repeated-games-against-budg.tldr: Known constraints on an adversary's action sequence enable efficiently computable minimax strategies through a random-playout method.

paragraphs: An artificial agent may have limitations that prevent it from pursuing a designer's objective effectively. In that situation, giving the agent a different immediate objective can sometimes help the designer obtain better results. Within reinforcement learning, this creates an optimization problem over the agent's reward function: which rewards produce useful behavior from this particular agent?

The paper develops a gradient-ascent method for approximately solving this reward-design problem during the agent's lifetime. The approach uses experience gained online and takes advantage of knowledge about the agent's structure. Reward design thereby becomes an ongoing learning process, informed by how the agent operates and what happens during its interaction with the environment.

The authors provide formal convergence guarantees and show that the method generalizes a standard policy-gradient approach. They also demonstrate improvements to reward functions for agents with different kinds of limitations. The findings support adapting rewards to an agent's capabilities, while the stated optimization goal remains an approximate solution to the optimal-reward problem.
neurips-2010-reward-design-via-online-gr.tldr: Online gradient ascent adapts an agent's reward function to its limitations, with convergence guarantees for approximately solving the reward-design problem.

paragraphs: A neural network's present state can retain traces of past inputs. Earlier analysis of linear networks driven by Gaussian input sequences placed a limit on memory duration tied to the number of neurons, measured in neuronal time constants. This paper examines how that picture changes when the input sequence is sparse.

For sparse inputs, the authors show that linear neural networks can effectively perform compressed sensing of their past inputs. A class of orthogonal recurrent networks can thereby achieve memory capacity exceeding the number of neurons. The enhancement depends on both the signal structure and the network class: the abstract does not attribute it to feedforward networks or generic recurrent networks.

Using methods from the statistical physics of disordered systems, the paper analytically computes memory-trace decay as a function of network size, sparsity, and integration time. From the compressed-sensing perspective, the same work introduces measurement matrices generated by dynamical systems and analyzes their asymptotic performance. The results connect short-term memory capacity to the structure of both inputs and recurrent dynamics.
neurips-2010-short-term-memory-in-neuron.tldr: For sparse inputs, orthogonal recurrent linear networks can use dynamical compressed sensing to achieve memory capacity beyond their neuron count.

paragraphs: Clustering is usually framed as an unsupervised task, but a teacher can provide information about the grouping a learner should recover. This paper studies a formal supervised-clustering framework with that kind of interaction. It gives an improved generic algorithm for any concept class within the model, emphasizing how little interaction with the teacher is needed.

The authors also extend the framework in two directions. The original model assumes perfect teacher responses; a noisy version relaxes this assumption, with an algorithm provided for the class of intervals. A separate dynamic model lets the teacher see a random subset of the points. These extensions distinguish different ways that access to supervision can be restricted.

Finally, the paper derives query bounds for datasets satisfying properties that range from weak to strong. Under the strongest property, a class of clustering functions that includes Single-Linkage finds the target clustering. The results connect the amount of supervision required to dataset structure, while keeping the broad generic result separate from the more specialized guarantees.
neurips-2010-supervised-clustering-841ef.tldr: The paper improves query-efficient supervised clustering and develops noisy and dynamic teacher models with additional conditional guarantees.

paragraphs: Neural activity can switch between states even when the change is not simply a jump in average firing rate. This paper introduces a switching state-space model that jointly estimates state transitions, the number of states, and firing rates that vary over time. It can detect changes in temporal firing patterns, including temporal correlation.

Because spikes are binary events, the model is non-Gaussian. The authors derive a variational Bayes algorithm for inference in this setting. Synthetic-data analysis reports strong performance relative to previous methods across the three estimation tasks. Joint estimation links the identification of states to the changing firing-rate dynamics used to characterize them.

The paper also analyzes recordings from the medial temporal area. The detected states probably correspond to transient and sustained states previously identified heuristically. Estimated parameters suggest that the transition is detected through a discontinuity in temporal correlation, a change previous methods could not detect. This offers evidence of practical benefit while keeping the biological interpretation and inferred detection mechanism appropriately tentative.
neurips-2010-switching-state-space-model.tldr: A switching state-space model jointly estimates neural states and changing firing rates, detecting transitions through temporal patterns as well as mean-rate changes.

paragraphs: When many people label images, their judgments can be noisy and their abilities can differ across kinds of images. This paper develops a method for estimating underlying image labels while representing those differences explicitly. Its model describes both the image-formation process and how annotators produce their responses.

Images have characteristics represented in an abstract Euclidean space. Annotators have multidimensional descriptions of competence, expertise, and bias. This allows the model to discover groups of people with different skills or knowledge, together with groups of images that differ qualitatively. The approach can therefore account for variation that would be obscured by treating annotator ability as a single uniform property.

On synthetic and real data, the model predicts ground-truth labels more accurately than the compared state-of-the-art methods. Experiments also show that binary annotations may contain enough information to reveal different schools of thought among annotators and group images from separate categories. The model thus uses disagreement both to improve label estimation and to uncover structure in the annotation process.
neurips-2010-the-multidimensional-wisdom.tldr: Modeling annotators' multidimensional expertise and bias improves label aggregation and can reveal groups of annotators and images.

paragraphs: Consistency concerns whether a learning method approaches the best achievable classification performance as the amount of training data grows. Universal consistency asks for this statistical property across data distributions within the theorem's scope. Earlier work established such a result for the standard binary support vector machine, leaving the multiclass setting as a separate theoretical question.

This paper proves universal consistency for the multiclass support vector machine formulated by Crammer and Singer. The proof extends techniques previously used for binary SVM classification to the case of more than two classes. Its contribution is therefore a statistical guarantee for a specific multiclass formulation, obtained by broadening an existing proof approach.

The result counters a prevailing belief, motivated by earlier analysis, that several multiclass SVM extensions were inconsistent. It establishes that the Crammer–Singer method has the stated asymptotic learning property. This is a claim about behavior as data accumulate, and its significance lies in clarifying the theoretical status of that method rather than reporting a finite-dataset performance comparison.
neurips-2010-universal-consistency-of-mu.tldr: The paper proves universal consistency for the Crammer–Singer multiclass SVM by extending proof techniques from binary classification.

paragraphs: Recognizing an action in a single image can require more than identifying a person's pose. Different actions may involve similar poses, with the decisive evidence lying in relationships between objects and body parts. This paper proposes using the actor's detected body parts to guide which local visual evidence the recognition system examines.

The method applies two stages to both training and test images. First, it detects the body parts relevant to the action, establishing a prior over useful local evidence. Second, it extracts features anchored to those parts and uses both the features and their relationships to the parts for classification. The body therefore provides a spatial reference for interpreting the image.

The authors state that these priors apply across a broad range of human actions. By directing attention toward relevant regions and relationships, the approach substantially simplifies learning and improves recognition performance. The contribution is a structured way to use body localization as guidance for action recognition from a still image.
neurips-2010-using-body-anchored-priors-.tldr: Detecting body parts first helps a single-image action recognizer focus on relevant features and their relationships to the actor.

paragraphs: Languages differ in their usual ordering of sentence elements, but the possible orders are not equally common. This paper seeks an information-theoretic explanation for that uneven distribution. It builds on Uniform Information Density, the idea that information content is distributed approximately evenly as a sentence unfolds.

The authors suggest that object-first languages are particularly disfavored because those orders distribute information poorly under this objective. The explanatory step is to evaluate word order in terms of how it spreads information through a sentence. They further argue that the frequency pattern among the remaining orders is at least partly explainable through the same principle, without claiming that it provides a complete account.

The paper supports its theoretical analysis with child-directed speech data and experimental work. These sources provide evidence for the proposed connection between information distribution and cross-language word-order patterns. The findings position uniform information density as a possible contributor to the observed preferences, especially the relative rarity of object-first orders.
neurips-2010-why-are-some-word-orders-mo.tldr: The paper argues that more even information distribution may partly explain word-order frequencies, especially the rarity of object-first languages.
